newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dutch to float draft EU treaty.
newsitem.headline: Dutch to float draft EU treaty.

text.p: The Netherlands, buoyed by the arrival of a more pro-European Union government in Britain, will hand its EU partners a new draft treaty for the bloc on Friday, hoping to wrap up a final deal on schedule in June.
EU sources said the Dutch, who hold the presidency of the 15 nation bloc for the first half of this year, will hand out the draft in Maastricht when negotiators meet for a two-day session.
But they said that the issue was considered so sensitive that the draft would be taken back after it had been circulated among the negotiators so that it was not leaked to the media.
One EU source said the Dutch had said there would be no copying machines provided. Another joked that the treaty was going to be handed out surreptitiously "in brown paper bags".

The meeting has been called to prepare for two higher level negotiating sessions next week -- the first with EU foreign ministers on Tuesday in the Hague, the second with heads of state and government in the Dutch resort of Noordwijk on Friday.

The aim of both meetings is to give a political boost to the negotiations, known as the inter-governmental conference (IGC), so that a new treaty can be signed at the EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.

Designed to prepare the bloc for enlargement, the new treaty is expected to make relatively minor changes to the way the EU works -- certainly when compared with previous treaties that created the single market and a blueprint for a single currency.
Its centrepiece will be creation by 2002 of what is being dubbed an area of freedom and security.
Changes will also be made to the way the EU takes decisions, with some dillution of national vetoes and a reweighting of votes in favour of larger EU countries.

Job creation and the environment will be given special legal standing as areas of concern to the bloc. Flexibility will be introduced in some form to allow some countries to integrate faster than others.
In addition, the bloc's existing procedures for forging common foreign and judicial policies is likely to be beefed up.
Optimism has grown in EU capitals in recent weeks that a new treaty can now be agreed at the Amsterdam summit following the election in Britain of a new Labour government.
The former Conservative government was vehemently opposed to many of the issues favoured by its partners and had threatened to block the treaty if it did not get its way in a number of areas.

Prime Minister Tony Blair's new government has taken a much more mainstream stance to the treaty changes, lifting threats of a veto and agreeing to join in with its partners in a number of key areas, such as on employment and the environment.
Although Britain remains opposed to some proposals -- for example over the incorporation into the EU of the Western European Union defence arm -- it is no longer isolated.
As they enter the final stage, meanwhile, the focus of negotiations has begun shifting towards the most politically sensitive items on the table.
These include whether every country should have a commissioner and whether a system should be created to give more clout to countries with larger populations.
